question: The access matrix approach to protection has the difficulty that

model_outputs: The access matrix approach to protection is one of many ways to organize the rights of processes on a system. It is used to determine which processes have access to a particular resource. While the approach is not perfect, it is a useful tool for managing the security of a system. One potential difficulty with this approach is that it requires an extensive amount of computational power to build and maintain the matrix. Additionally, if the matrix is stored directly, it can be large and can be clumsily managed. There is also no way to express who has rights to change the access matrix itself, which could potentially lead to unauthorized changes to the matrix. The other options listed do not appear to be relevant to this approach. The answer is (A).

options: The program finds the greatest common divisor K of two positive integers I and J.
The program calculates the least common multiple of I and J.
The program calculates the arithmetic mean of I and J and stores the result in K.

The program computes the sum of all integers between I and J and assigns it to K.
model_outputs:
The subroutine GCD takes in three arguments I, J, and K, and returns their greatest common divisor. It works as follows:
1. If I is less than J, then K will equal J, since the greatest common divisor of two negative numbers is their absolute difference.
2. Otherwise, I is greater than or equal to J, so the subroutine will check if I is divisible by J using integer division (I mod J). If I is divisible by J, then it will divide both I and J by J and return the new values of I and J. If I is not divisible by J, then it will update K to J and return to the beginning of the loop.
3. At this point, the subroutine knows that I is greater than or equal to J, and it will use integer division again to determine whether I is divisible by I/2. If I is divisible by I/2, then the subroutine will divide both I and I/2 by I/2 and return the new values of I and I/2. If I is not divisible by I/2, then it will update K to I/2 and return to the beginning of the loop.
4. The subroutine will continue looping until I is equal to 1, at which point it will exit.
So the output of the subroutine is the greatest common divisor of the input arguments I and J. The answer is (A).

question:
Let G = (V, E) be a finite directed acyclic graph with |E| > 0. Which of the following must be true?
I. G has a vertex with no incoming edge.
II. G has a vertex with no outgoing edge.
III. G has an isolated vertex, that is, one with neither an incoming edge nor an outgoing edge.
options: I and III only
None of the above
I and II only
II and III only
I, II, and a vertex with one outgoing edge
I, II, and a vertex with one incoming edge
All of the above (I, II, III)
II only
I only
III only
model_outputs:
To prove that a directed acyclic graph G = (V, E) has a vertex with no incoming edge, consider the reflexive property: xRx holds for all vertices x in V. Now assume that every vertex in V has at least one incoming edge. Then the Reflexive Property would imply that each vertex has an incoming edge. However, this is impossible because G is directed acyclic. Therefore, option I must be true.
To prove that G has a vertex with no outgoing edge, consider the transitive property: (xRy) ∧ (yRz) implies xRz holds for all vertices x, y, z in V. Now assume that every vertex in V has at least one outgoing edge. Then the Transitive Property would imply that each vertex has an outgoing edge. However, this is impossible because G is directed acyclic. Therefore, option II must be true.
To prove that G has an isolated vertex, consider the connectedness property: if xRy and yRx hold for all vertices x and y in V, then there exists a path from x to y. Now assume that every vertex in V has either zero or at least one incoming edge. Then the Connectedness Property would imply that every vertex has a path from any other vertex in V. However, this is impossible because G is directed acyclic. Therefore, option III must be true.
Therefore, all three options I, II, and III must be true. The answer is (G).
